speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: GREAT SEAL
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CHANGE IN DESIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to inform the house that Her Majesty the Queen has approved the adoption and use by the government of Canada of a new Great Seal of Canada.
Since confederation the design of every Great Seal of Canada has comprised the effigy of the reigning sovereign seated on the throne, crowned and robed, and holding in each hand the orb and sceptre, or sword; also the Canadian armorial bearings, and around the rim an inscription of the title and name of the sovereign. The design of the new Great Seal which Her Majesty has now approved is of this design, with the bilingual inscription "Elizabeth II Queen of Canada-Reine du Canada".
The design shows Her Majesty wearing the St. Edward's crown with which the Queen was crowned at Westminster, and this crown also surmounts the whole armorial bearings of Canada, in addition to being part of the crest.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, February 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. 82, to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain- Mr. Howe (Port Arthur)-Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
On clause 3-Minister's liability to a bank.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Order. May I take the liberty of pointing out to hon. members that it is unfair to expect any member of the house to open this discussion with the noise that has been going on. I know that there is always this little disturbance while we get settled down, but let us please keep it as quiet as possible, because one of these times it may be ourselves who wish to speak, and I think we should extend the same courtesy to others as we would expect them to extend to us.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could make a comment or two in regard to subclause (1) (e) (ii) at the bottom of page 2. This reads:
fifteen hundred dollars, minus the aggregate, at the time of the application for the loan, of the moneys that have been paid or are payable for the sale of grain delivered by or on behalf of the borrower under his current permit book before the making of the loan and on or after the 1st day of August, 1955, other than for grain delivered and entered in the permit book as the balance of the 1954-55 eight bushel quota.

Grain
I wonder if the minister would indicate how the owner of the land might be eligible if he has been renting it. Common practice has been for a farmer, when he retires, to rent his land to his son or to a neighbour so that the owner pays the taxes and the renter pays one-third of the crop to the landlord if and when it is sold. Let us take a typical case where the crop is 6,000 bushels. The landlord is entitled to 2,000 bushels, and the renter has 4,000 bushels, out of which he must pay all operating costs, but the landlord must pay his taxes. At the present time the landlord will have difficulty in getting any cash until the renter has been able to market at least eight or ten bushels per acre. I wonder if the minister could indicate what provision, if any, has been made for the owner of the land to receive assistance under the subclause I have just mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I thought I had made it clear that only the actual producer of the grain is entitled to borrow under this bill. The relations between the owner and his tenant are whatever they are under the law; but, so far as this bill is concerned, only the producer can borrow.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: As I pointed out, the landlord is committed to pay the taxes. That is an essential part of the operation of any farm. Normally the tenant would deliver to the landlord his third of the crop by Christmas time, but under the present set-up the tenant must have at least 5 bushels per acre to meet actual cash disbursements. It seems to me that quite a large number of the owners of the 200,000 farm units in the prairie provinces are retired. They are too old to work the land and do not have a permit book. It seems to me there should be some provision for them. If a retired farmer has 2,000 bushels of grain which cannot be delivered it should be possible for him to get some assistance so that he can aieet his taxes and pay his grocery bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It seems to me that my hon. friend is putting up a straw man. If the tenant could deliver his grain freely he would give the farmer one-third of the money. If he borrows from the bank I suppose he can still give the farmer one-third of the money. The position is unchanged. The regulation is exactly the same as in the 1951 bill, and I am told that no single instance of the kind mentioned by my hon. friend was ever raised.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say a word on this clause. If I interpret paragraph (e) (ii) of subclause 1 correctly, $1,500 is the maximum amount that a producer can get. I also understand that if a
IMr. Nicholson.]
producer has sold grain to the value of $1,000 he would only be entitled to an additional $500. If that is so I think it should be changed so that once the legislation comes into effect the producer may be entitled to get the full $1,500 regardless of whether or not he has in the past sold a few bushels of grain. As far as I can see, it should not make any difference whether he has already sold some grain before the coming into effect of the legislation. He should still be entitled to the full $1,500.
The bank is not bestowing a favour on the producer. The bank is carrying on a legitimate business for which they are being paid a fairly handsome rate of interest with an absolute guarantee. Therefore it seems to me that this is an imposition on the producer and he should be allowed to get the full $1,500 when the legislation is passed regardless of whether or not he has previously sold any grain.
Mr. Hansel!: I should like to call attention to paragraph (d) of subclause 1 in which the rate of interest of 5 per cent is mentioned. Yesterday the hon. member for Acadia rose and put in rather concise form the fact that the government was in an excellent position to persuade the banks to grant these loans at cost. I agree with that and I do so on this basis. After all, I take it that the purpose of this piece of legislation is to meet an emergency. If an emergency had not arisen there would be no need for the bill. I am not going into a detailed discussion on that point. We all know the background and the reasons for the bill. The farmers have claimed that they need money by reason that they cannot sell their grain. Part of the responsibility for disposal of the farmers' grain falls on the government.
Now then, the government recognizes that this emergency exists and they have introduced this bill. But the fact remains that the farmers are going to be burdened with 5 per cent interest on a tragedy for which they are not responsible. Because of these circumstances we believe that it would not be unreasonable that in emergency legislation of this kind the banks be asked to lend money at cost. The other feature is that the banks are going to be guaranteed against loss. There will be very few losses sustained when the government, through this legislation, is going to guarantee the banks against loss.
Now, let me read what the hon. member for Acadia said yesterday at page 1507 of Hansard, the second column:
That is why some of us wonder whether or not the government endeavoured to get the chartered banks to make loans at a lower rate than 5 per cent where the loans are guaranteed by the government.

Grain
Now, I will skip a piece here lor the sake of brevity and read from the middle of the page. The hon. member for Acadia said:
Remember that some years ago we had Mr. Towers before the banking committee, and he told us that he estimated it cost the banks approximately 3 per cent to create money. If it costs the banks 3 per cent to create money, then surely on loans guaranteed by the government they should be prepared to make loans at cost. As has already been pointed out, they are making loans at cost, if 3 per cent is the cost, to the wheat board, and they are making loans to the wheat pools at approximately 32 per cent, just three-quarters of one per cent above their cost as estimated by the former governor of the Bank of Canada.
Now, the following sentence is the pertinent one:
In view of that fact, I think it would be interesting to know whether or not the government did attempt to get the banks to make loans at a lower rate than 5 per cent.
Then the hon. member for York West spoke. The government did not answer that question, and I think it would be interesting to know, in their talks with the representatives of the chartered banks, as to whether or not the banks were willing to grant loans at cost or grant loans at 3 per cent or 4 per cent, and what persuasive arguments the government used by reason of the emergency to ask the banks to grant loans at cost. I think that question should be answered and therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am going to move an amendment. It is a simple one. I move:
That section 3 subsection (1), clause (d) be amended by deleting the words "five per cent", and substituting therefor the words "three per cent".

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is quite impossible to do that because that would be imposing a unilateral change in an agreement. In other words, there is an agreement between the banks and the government and it has been outstanding for some time. The banks have lent large sums of money on the strength of the exchange of letters with the Minister of Finance. Personally, neither myself nor this party will agree to repudiate the signature of the Minister of Finance which is the signature of the government of Canada. If my hon. friend thinks that is good Social Credit practice we of the Liberal party do not believe it is sound government practice.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think that is the question at issue, if I may say so with all due respect to the minister. That is not the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Order. I see the hon. member for Macleod.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know the minister is aggravated. The debate has been going on for a long time, and we are now on
a very important section of the bill. But I think that the minister's interjection "if that is good Social Credit practice" is entirely uncalled for. I will tell the minister what good Social Credit practice would be, and that is to bring down a bill and get the authority of parliament before striking an agreement with anyone else. That is what good Social Credit practice would be, and the people of this country should know now that Social Credit members would not override the authority of parliament.
Here is the point, Mr. Chairman. Many hon. members on this side of the house have risen and called attention to the government's flouting of the powers of parliament. Is there an agreement existing between the government and the banks? If there is an agreement existing between the government and the banks, then parliament becomes a rubber stamp.
I can understand how there could be an exchange of letters. That might be all right. I hope there is an exchange of letters between some other interested parties and the government as well as with the banks. The situation is this. The bill is now before us. We are discussing the bill. The committee has a right to amend any bill. It is my proposal that we amend this bill now. I cannot help how impractical it may appear to change the bill. If the government has made any mistake, that is its responsibility, not parliament's. We are saying what kind of bill we want now. This is not even the kind of bill we have been continually advocating. By reason of the defeats of previous amendments we are now forced into the position where we must fight for the best bill possible. We want to pass legislation which we believe in the circumstances is the best piece of legislation obtainable, and we claim now that the interest rate should be 3 per cent instead of 5 per cent. Therefore, we have moved this amendment, and the committee will have to deal with it regardless of whether or not the government stuck its neck out and reached some agreement with the banks. But I must confess I do not like this idea of governments making agreements and then bringing the bills here to be passed and then saying: "You have got to pass it because we have made the agreement".

The Minister of Trade and Commerce in his latest outburst has introduced the ugly word "repudiation". It is a fantastic use of the word as applied to what is under discussion. This is not a case where any valid obligation binding on the government of Canada is being repudiated or is proposed to be repudiated. If it were I am sure those of us who are members of the official opposition would have nothing to do with it. We do not believe in repudiation; we always have opposed any proposal of repudiation. But the minister is completely mistaken in suggesting that there is now binding upon the people of Canada through the government of Canada any legal obligation. The only obligation that has been created in any sense whatever is the obligation which the government took upon itself by means of a letter written by the Minister of Finance to the banks of this country saying that legislation would be introduced. That is the only obligation there was. There was a moral obligation placed upon the government by that letter, but no legal obligation was created by it. The only kind of legal obligation that could be created would be one created by parliament. The government is asking us to create it, but the minister in this remarkable and silly statement he has made this morning about repudiation, assumes that a legal obligation is in existence now. We have reached the point where the minister is resorting to these utterly fantastic suggestions and charges in order to buttress a position which is so hopelessly weak. He does not attract any strength to the position by resorting to far-fetched suggestions of this kind.
There is no legal obligation in existence today as far as the people or the government of Canada are concerned. Only parliament can create any legal obligation, and that has not yet been done. So let there be none of this silly talk about repudiation as applied to what parliament is engaged in doing now, namely, deciding whether it shall permit the government to create a legal obligation and what shall be the terms of such legal obligation. We have a perfectly free hand in this parliament to decide on what terms we will permit the government to undertake such obligation.
Having been the person who raised the question last evening as to what discussions had been carried on by the government with the banks of Canada in relation to the interest rate, I wish to follow that up with one or two brief observations. I drew attention last

Grain
night to the fact that there are a good many people who would be happy to lend money with a guarantee of the government of Canada for an interest rate substantially less than 5 per cent.
There are two kinds of obligation that we have to consider here in a reasonable approach to a question of this kind. There are shortterm obligations and there are term obligations. The government of Canada borrows money today on 10-year maturities through savings bonds at a rate of 3J per cent. Presumably an obligation with similar maturity terms guaranteed by the government would yield a similar return.
Here we are dealing with short-term obligations. The government guarantee is applied to an obligation which will mature in the ordinary sense in six months, as the minister indicated in his explanation last night. In that field the government today is borrowing at substantially less than the 3| per cent which is being paid by the government on 10-year maturities or on maturities of more than 10 years.
On the other hand, in a situation of this kind we have to make some allowance for handling charges. This is not simply a case of the government selling bonds. Some account has to be taken of the fact that these applications for loans must be processed, the bank must make certain investigations, certain prescribed forms must be completed and paper work will have to be done by the bank and in its contact with the government in order to put the guarantee into full effect. Anybody who believes in the scheme of this bill must take account of the fact that something must be allowed to the banks for handling charges.
But this does not yet provide an answer to the question that was asked last night. I think the Minister of Finance was here at the time or at least he had been here just before. He took his departure then and he has not appeared since in this committee of the whole during the discussion of this bill, as I think he should. He is the man who carried on the negotiations with the banks- and after I asked the question the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he did not have anything to do with the banks, and it was the Minister of Finance who had carried on these negotiations. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he did not know what discussions the Minister of Finance had had with the banks about a proper interest rate. So the question remains unanswered because the Minister of Finance has not chosen to be in the committee or to acquaint the committee with the facts. an answer to the question before it deals with the clause and before it deals with this amendment. This committee is entitled to know what was the course of discussion between the government and the banks in regard to the interest rate.
I am sure that the Minister of Finance does not just write a letter out of the blue offering to introduce a bill to provide government guarantees for a scheme of bank loans. Surely the matter of interest rates must have entered into these discussions and before this house takes one step further it ought to be told in the plainest terms by the Minister of Finance what were the discussions and what was the position taken by the banks in regard to the maximum interest rate at which they were prepared to lend. We ought to know what was the government's position. Did the government make any serious effort to obtain for the farmers who will be borrowing under this measure an interest rate lower than the 5 per cent now contemplated?
I suggest to (the government that the Minister of Finance should be sent for. He should come into the committee now and answer that question. This house has no right to go ahead passing a measure of this kind in relation to something that is going to be most important for the borrowers without having that information.

Mr. Chairman, this is an issue which is a little different from a mere question whether three per cent or any other particular percentage is an appropriate amount. What has practically been placed before us as the issue upon which we must vote is whether or not we have the right to vary any provision of this act.
The minister has propounded a doctrine that, because the government committed itself to certain arrangements without consulting parliament we are therefore bound to the detail of those arrangements. I submit that we have not before us the evidence that would make it clear whether or not three per cent is the figure that could appropriately be charged, but I am satisfied that the minister has made the issue here whether we have or have not the right to vary any provision of this bill.

I must say that I do not know-and I do not think any other hon. member knows, including the member who moves this amendment-whether in fact three per cent is the appropriate figure. From day to day the amounts that must be charged by government vary. However, the minister has put this on the ground that we have no right to challenge the rate of five per cent because this government has committed itself to the banks and therefore we must abide by that decision. If that principle were to be accepted, all that would be necessary for the government to do in any case would be to abandon the ordinary procedure, enter into improper arrangements in advance of the meeting of parliament, make commitments to various corporations or other bodies in this country and then come before parliament and say, "Because we have done this, you cannot discuss any variation. We are pledged, and it must ride or fall in detail as we have put it before you." That would deny to this parliament the right of discussion, which is the very foundation of parliamentary democracy. That, I think, is an issue which the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not understand, but he has made that the issue in the amendment that is now before us.
I am reluctant to support an amendment setting forth an exact figure which does not have supporting evidence to tell us whether or not it would be the right amount. But I am prepared to support this amendment as a challenge to the statement of the minister that they have made the commitment for five per cent and that stands no matter what the effects are. On that ground I shall certainly support this amendment as an acceptance of the challenge that parliament has no right to vary any figure in this bill.
I think also that the minister has made a statement here that should not go without notice. He said just a few minutes ago that the government must endorse the decision of a member of the government. We have had brought before us here, by a steady process of prodding and prying and questioning, decisions by various ministers that were unknown to the other ministers. If they were going to follow the course of being committed in every case to what is done by those ministers without the knowledge of the other ministers, then we would indeed have reached a point where parliament would be impotent to guide the affairs of this country. That would apply with more force to the members opposite than to the opposition. It would be the responsibility of the members opposite in particular to challenge a proposition of that kind. That proposition would mean that every hon. member opposite who supports this 67509-97i
government is reduced to the role of a rubber stamp and that by his unquestioning vote he denies to this parliament the real freedom of discussion and the formation of opinion which should decide the course of legislation in this parliament of Canada. Reference has been made to the undertaking which the government gave to the banks. The minister said earlier that the government and the Liberal party would stand behind that undertaking. He has confirmed that view now by saying to the Leader of the Opposition that he cannot command enough votes to change the views of the government. In other words, the minister is quite satisfied that those on his side of the house will stand by the government so far as this matter is concerned.
I think it should be pointed out that the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other members of the government have lived up to the undertaking they gave to the banks. Three letters were written to Mr. F. W. Nicks, president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, the Bank of Nova Scotia, Toronto, Ontario.
This evidence is found in three letters which are contained in sessional paper No. 189 which was laid on the table of the house on Monday, February 13. The letters were written on October 28, 1955, November 25, 1955, and January 20, 1956. I want to read only short extracts from one or two of them. In the first letter which was signed by the Minister of Finance there appears this paragraph:
I am authorized to inform you that legislation in some respects similar to the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act 1951, will be introduced in parliament at the earliest opportunity to provide for a guarantee by the Minister of

Grain
Finance to the chartered banks of loans made under section 88 of the Bank Act and subject to the following additional conditions . . .
I will not read the conditions. There are about two pages of them. The concluding paragraph in the first letter reads as follows:
Loans made by the banks in advance of the legislation under the terms and conditions above described will become guaranteed loans when the legislation comes into force, and I should appreciate your confirmation that, in the meantime, the banks will participate in making such loans.
Those are the only two references in that first letter to anything that might be called an undertaking. The government undertook to introduce legislation. That is all they undertook to do. I think the letter was poorly worded in the last paragraph when the Minister of Finance used the phrase "when the legislation comes into force." I think he should have had enough respect for the rights of parliament at least to say, "if and when the legislation comes into force."

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, my hon. friends opposite laugh at our concern for the niceties of parliament but the niceties of parliamentary procedure are important. The other two letters, those dated November 25, 1955, and January 20, 1956, indicate changes that were made in the proposed legislation, and all they say that bears on the point now being discussed is that the Minister of Finance is authorized to inform the banks that the legislation to be introduced will be along certain lines. Surely it is clear, Mr. Chairman, that the only undertaking the minister gave to the banks was that legislation would be introduced. That has been done, but surely parliament has the say as to what should happen to that legislation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say a word with regard to the rate of interest. In promising to introduce this legislation the government was doing as the farm leaders asked them to do at that time, and naturally they wanted a workable system introduced. There is no use introducing a system whereby the banks would not get a guarantee unless they lent money at a rate of interest at which they would lose money. In other words, if you set the rate of interest too low it would mean that you would be putting a plan into effect that would not work at all. Therefore the only question so far as I am concerned is whether the rate of interest has been set as low as it possibly can be and expect the plan to work.
On that basis I remember what happened when we were putting through the Farm Improvement Loans Act. At that time some

of us felt the rate ot interest should be lower that 5 per cent. We heard a great deal of evidence and it all went to show that if the rate were set at 4 per cent the banks could not lend at that rate without losing money. They pointed out that if we put the rate of interest at 4 per cent we might just as well not pass the bill because nobody would be able to borrow money under it at that rate.
The majority of the members on that committee came to the conclusion that, although they would have liked to see a lower rate because there was a partial government guarantee, it was more important to the farmer to be able to get money to improve his farm and buy machinery and so on at 5 per cent than for them to make heroes of themselves by setting the rate at 4 per cent with the result that the farmer would not get any money at all. That is why the rate was set at 5 per cent, and obviously when it was set at 5 per cent at that time it was based upon the cost of doing business of the banks and of the money.
A little over one year ago this whole question of cost of making small loans was dealt with in the banking and commerce committee where we had evidence of the experience of the Canadian Bank of Commerce in making small loans. I should like to refer quickly to the evidence given there. During the year ended October 31, 1953, the average amount of loans was $515. During the whole period the plan had been in operation the average amount was smaller than that but that was the average during that year. The bank was charging an effective rate of interest of 10 [DOT] 46 per cent, almost 10J per cent. Against the plan it charged 2-05 per cent as the cost of providing the money, so it was not charging a high rate for the cost of the money.
In spite of only charging roughly 2 per cent, the cost of doing business in making small loans was such that their operating profit before income tax was 1-46 per cent. In other words, while they charged only 2 per cent against their banking operations for the money they put into the small loan plan, after taking into account the cost of making these small loans their operating profit before income tax was 1-46 per cent. The cost of operation in making these loans in small amounts was such that even though they charged 10-46 per cent to the borrower and were only getting interest at 2 per cent representing the cost of providing the money they only had a profit of 1-46 per cent.
If you take what the bank got out of it by way of interest and profit, 2 per cent and 1-46 per cent, they got 3-46 per cent and

charged 10-46 per cent. So according to the actual figures it was costing the bank 7 per cent to conduct this business. That is 7 per cent over interest. I grant that if loans average more than $500, as they probably will be in this case, it will cut down the cost of doing business, but I ask hon. members this question. If, over and above the cost of the money, it costs the bank up to 7 per cent to administer a small loan plan of this type, even with a low rate of interest of roughly 2 per cent, then are the banks not going to say that they will lose money if we only give them 1 per cent over the 2 per cent representing the cost of the money to do business and will there be any money lent at all when, according to the evidence, it cost them 7 per cent to engage in the small loan business over and above the cost of the money?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Surely.

speechtext: There was no guarantee of those loans by the government and, second, there was no advertising of the loans and therefore no advertising expense.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: And third, they are not secured.

speechtext:
The amount spent on advertising by Canadian Bank of Commerce was only [DOT]15 per cent, just a little over one-tenth of one per cent. So that does not affect the argument. With regard to the partial guarantee, obviously if you say to the banks that you will guarantee them against losses but will only let them collect a rate of interest on which they are going to lose money on every bit of business they do, then you might just as well kill the bill. Everybody must know that. In trying to get a deal with the banks whereby the farmers would get some money the government had to make a deal whereby the banks were likely to lend some money, and had the government done differently the farmers of western Canada would have had a right to complain.
I think I understand the situation of the farmers of western Canada. They need money to meet their living expenses and so on. A rate of 2 per cent on $1,500 for six months would be $15.
I do not think that any farmer would appreciate it or thank us for saying that we are so worried about wanting to save you some interest we are going to prevent you from paying that $15 of extra interest, even if it means you will not get any money at all. If my hon. friends opposite really believe that the farmers need money to carry them
Grain
over, surely they would not vote for an amendment that would mean this bill was, in effect, killed and the farmers would not be able to get any money at all under the plan. I will have no hesitation in voting against this amendment because the effect of the amendment would be to say to the farmer, we are being so concerned about you that we are going to say you cannot borrow at all. Of course, we will cover it up by advancing the idea we are in favour of low interest rates.
I believe in facing the facts. We have the experience under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the evidence given to the banking and commerce committee in regard to the Small Loans Act. In the light of the evidence that has been put before the banking and commerce committee over and over again, nobody could suggest that the banks could hope to engage in this business at 3 per cent without losing a lot of money. Then, do my hon. friends opposite say that if the banks are invited to go into the lending business at a point where they are going to lose a lot of money they are going to put out money to the extent required by the farmers? They know themselves that the effect of carrying this amendment would mean that the farmers would get no more money under this plan. Is that what they want? Well, it is not what I want. I should like to see the farmers receive the benefits the government intended them to receive under this legislation, and at a reasonable rate of interest for small loans, namely 5 per cent. I have no hesitation in saying that I intend to vote against this amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to use a term that was coined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, this is rapidly degenerating into a debate. There are one or two things that have been said by the hon. member for Rosthern that require some comment. First of all, there is one correction, and that is that the act that was being considered by the banking and commerce committee was not the Small Loans Act, but the Bank Act. There is also the fact that the kind of loans that were being considered were very different from these. There was no guarantee. There was no security such as there is in this case. In addition to that there was the very large cost of advertising and solicitation to get the loans. The position is not at all comparable.
I have said, without any reservation, that we have not the facts before us that would make it possible to determine exactly what the percentage should be. I view this amendment more in the light of an assertion that we have a right to demand an examination

Grain
of the interest rate, rather than a declaration that we know whether it should be 3 per cent or any other amount. I quite recognize that what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said is correct. We have the right of discussion, but it is more than the right of discussion that is involved. There at least must be the inference that the government is prepared to listen to arguments. After all, the right of discussion has no meaning in the light of the proposition put forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he said, we do not question that you have the right of discussion but we question whether you have the votes. In other words, it does not make any difference what you say; you go ahead and talk, but if we have the votes we will just simply go ahead. Of course, implicit in everything that has been said is that we will crack the whip and our followers will toe the line.
In this proposition there is more than the substance of the amendment. It is a question of whether discussion in this house is still an attempt to try to reach some reasonable conclusion. We have put forward a proposition that has been dealt with, and I cannot suggest to you whether or not it was wise, that is that this should have been referred to a committee.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You are out of order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am not out of order at all. We would have provided an opportunity in that way. I still suggest to this government that in the light of the discussion that has taken place this morning they consider the advisability of providing an opportunity not only to the farmer representatives but to the representatives of the banks as well, so that we could have the facts before us in regard to this case. In so far as the argument used by the hon. member for Rosthern is concerned, I can only express some measure of satisfaction that he did not make that argument over television in western Canada or some more television sets might have been endangered as a result.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I find it very difficult to believe that the hon. member for Rosthern was really serious when he was trying to get us to believe that making loans under the small loans branch of banking is comparable to making loans under this legislation. The loans under the Small Loans Act are very small. They go down to $50. The average loan under this legislation to date is $800; that is a fairly large sized loan. Is he going to suggest that making loans of an average size of $800 is similar to making loans under the small loans branch, which is a very special' ized form of making loans? The fact is that

the small loan companies have been charging 2 per cent per month in the past and that shows a rate very much higher than general banking practice. The fact that the Bank of Commerce was charging around 10 per cent for small loans while they were charging an average of 5 per cent or 6 per cent on their general banking practice shows the big difference between the two.
As the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out, under the small loans branch the banks have the cost of investigation, the cost of a chattel mortgage and various things. Under this legislation they have wheat in the bins. In addition, the farmer goes to the banker and signs certain statements before the loans are made. Then the bank does not even have the cost of collection. The loans are collected by the elevator companies. The two are totally unrelated, therefore. Of course, on top of that the loans are guaranteed by the government. The hon. member should think twice, therefore, before he asks members in this house to believe in what I call the ridiculous suggestion he just made.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosthern has made a real plea in favour of what I consider to be a very high rate of interest. I do not believe his argument is well founded when he compares this legislation to the small loans legislation. His argument was not well founded according to his own words because he pointed out the cost of a small loan was somewhere around 7 per cent and therefore if loans under this legislation cost less the banks would be losing money. I do not believe even the hon. member for Rosthern thinks the banks are going to lose money under this legislation.
We are going to*support the amendment because it goes at least part of the way towards the end we have been attempting to accomplish. No one has said money could be made available without any cost. Loans or cash advances cannot be made available free, without some charge to somebody. But we have continuously said that there should be no charge to the producer. I take it the hon. member for Macleod is now saying that if we have lost the fight to have advances made without any cost at all, the next best thing is to attempt to get the 5 per cent reduced. On the other hand, the hon. member for Rosthern is arguing in favour of a high interest rate, namely 5 per cent. Some years ago he was well known for ideas about monetary reform. A large part of those ideas was to get interest rates down. He argued this morning to maintain high rates of interest. The hon. member for Rosthern is arguing that the full cost of any advance or any loan that

is made to the farmer, plus the profit involved, must be borne by him. If the amendment should carry there will be nothing to prevent the government from moving a further amendment to this legislation to make up any loss that might be incurred, if there should be any loss, and I am not convinced there would be at the rate of 3 per cent.
What the hon. member for Rosthern is arguing is that the farmer shall pay the whole shot. The hon. member for Macleod is saying that we at least should be making some contribution as the parliament of this nation toward seeing that the farmer gets a loan at a reasonable rate.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I wish to say a few words on this. When the hon. member for Rosthern was speaking I attempted to ask him a question but he did not want to be interrupted at that point.

high rate of 5 per cent interest, then I think there is every justification for the case that we have been trying to make that loans should be made through the Canadian wheat board, and that this government should give the responsibility and the power-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
It would appear from the discussion that is taking place at this time that the minister would have been well advised to have brought this to the committee on banking and commerce or the committee on agriculture and colonization either of which could properly have dealt with it; however, we must ask our questions here.
I was rather intrigued by the hon. member for Rosthern when I discovered he was persuading himself that the interest rate was perfectly justified especially when I read the act. I understand that the act was negotiated between the Minister of Finance and the banks.
Clause 3, sub-clause 1, paragraph (d) of the act specifically says the interest rate charged by the banks on the loan did not exceed 5 per cent per annum. That would indicate to me that it is not mandatory to charge 5 per cent and that the banks themselves recognize that they could have given interest at a rate lower than 5 per cent. Therefore I would suggest to the hon. member for whom we all have a great deal of respect that certainly he should have taken that little phrase, "did not exceed 5 per cent" into consideration before having made those particular remarks.
The hon. member for Kindersley earlier in the debate asked certain questions of the minister in respect to a quarter-section farmer and the minister in reply indicated that it would take longer than six months in some cases to repay this loan. However, the bill itself does not indicate that and there is no provision for that. I find here that the amount of the loan is payable on the first day of
October. If a quarter-section farmer makes a loan in May or June that does not provide a six months period and then the bank can come to the government and expect a repayment of the guaranteed loan. I was wondering if possibly the minister might elaborate somewhat on that point and indicate how we are protected against an instance such as that. Probably the farmer wishes to pay his bill but he does not have the money because he has not been able to deliver his wheat. The farmer is going to be put in the awkward position of having a loan come due and the banks, of course, can come to the government for the guarantee. Would the minister care to comment on that?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

All I am going to say on this particular point is that it is quite obvious to me that the government in its negotiations with the banks did not fight for low rates of interest. If there had been any controversy about it the Minister of Trade and Commerce would have known of it.
A further proof is this. In the return that was brought down, return No. 189, the first letter that was written on October 28 by the Minister of Finance to the president of the Canadian bankers' association states in the first paragraph:
May I refer to the negotiations that have been carried on between representatives of the chartered banks and representatives of the departments of finance and trade and commerce with a view to facilitating loans to grain producers in western Canada.
It then goes on to set out certain conditions, the third one being:
(iii) that interest on the loan does not exceed 5 per cent simple interest.
That was the first letter. I do not think there is much controversy there. In the second letter that was written certain changes were made, but there was no change in the interest rate. Some further changes were made in the third letter that was written but it contains no suggestion of any reduction in the rate of interest. I take it from that that the rate of interest was not a controversial matter, that the government did not fight for a lower rate of interest but simply suggested that 5 per cent was all right and they would let it go.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

On more than one occasion we were able to borrow money for as low as 2 per cent when we were putting in our water and sewer facilities. Mr. Chairman, I think the noisy people across the way are beginning to see how completely ridiculous their position is. When a government really wants to help people it goes to work and does something tor the people, not try to gouge them the way this bill does.
I should like to draw the attention of the hon. member for Rosthern to one or two facts which he knows very well. If the Bank of Canada has a $100 bond of the dominion government submitted to it, it can create $100 without its costing anybody anything. It could just as well be a $100,000 bond. If every dollar of the money to be loaned to farmers was obtained from the source from which the dominion government can get money, the Bank of Canada, that could be done by simply writing a Dominion of Canada bond and putting it in the hands of the Bank of Canada. I know the hon. member for Rosthern knows that. It is most important that every hon. member knows that and that the country knows that.
I should like to know whether the hon. member for Rosthern will take the untenable position that the dominion government should not have ample money created by the Bank of Canada in order to lend at 2 per cent.

speechtext: What are my hon. friends arguing about? The government has provided in this measure for guaranteed loans to farmers through the banks at a rate of interest of five per cent. I presume that, had a lower rate of interest been secured from the banks, the guarantee required would have had to be higher. I think that is logical and reasonable, and that is the approach that has been made here. Interest on a loan of $1,000 at five per cent for a period of six months, if I have calculated correctly, amounts to $25. If the same loan is secured at four per cent, it amounts to $20. What is this argument about between a four per cent and a five per cent loan? For a six months period on $1,000, it means $5. My hon. friends also argue on the basis that this money should have been provided through the wheat board. If that is their argument and if they maintain that the expense thereof should be borne by the wheat board, I say that is unfair as an item to be charged under operating expenses.

I am talking on the interest item on which you have been talking all morning. Some people will be borrowing by means of these bank loans, and others will not. It is wholly unfair to say that the man who does not need to borrow should pay the interest costs of the man who does need to borrow. I shall go one step further in the same regard on this item. I look to the man who may have some securities but has a right to borrow, under the argument of my hon. friends opposite, an interest-free loan, but I go further and I take the case of a man-there are many such-who may have a mortgage on his farm, on which he is paying interest. He is able to sell a certain amount of grain in his deliveries this fall and from that should have paid off his mortgage. But, instead of paying off his mortgage, he did not do so, but retained that money that he had secured from the sale of his grain for pocket money to pay expenses and so forth. Is anybody going to say that somebody else is to get an interest-free loan while that man is continuing to pay 5 or 6 per cent on the mortgage money he has borrowed? That to me seems wholly logical, and there is no argument on it.
I doubt very much if my hon. friends opposite could stir up very much interest in the country over the item of interest itself. When farmers get accommodation of this kind, I think they would be expected to pay interest on it. I simply come back to what I pointed out earlier, that the argument here

seems to be over a matter of $5, between a $1,000 loan for six months at 5 per cent as compared with the same loan for the same period of time at 4 per cent. That is all I wish to say on that.

The newer form does not have the same effect on the applicant as did the earlier one. Would the minister say what regulations, if any, have been passed as of this date? I should

Grain
also like to know whether any form or return is made by the banks under this or any other section setting out the names of applicants who have applied for loans and have been turned down.
I believe it was the minister who stated the other day he did not think there were very many. I have no idea of the numbers but I do know that in the course of the last three weeks I have received letters from 17 or 18 farmers who were turned down, who had on their premises the necessary wheat, but having advised the local bank manager as to the purposes for which they desired the money, namely the payment of some current liabilities other than for actual groceries and the like, the explanation given in these various cases was that these loans were not intended to cover instances such as were contemplated by the intended borrower. I should like the minister to give some kind of assurance because farmers are asking, what is this legislation? Why is it that unless an applicant is practically in a position where he could actually borrow on his own security, in certain branches of certain banks the application is being denied?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We have been told several times in this debate, Mr. Chairman, that we cannot have regulations when the bill has not been approved.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: But you have tentative ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
We have tentative ones. I am told that the forms that are used for applications for loans and certain other forms were tabled in the house this morning in the usual way. My hon. friend says that people who have the required amount of wheat have been turned down. I should like to know what the other circumstances were, how many liens were filed on the wheat. So far as the government is concerned, the two requirements are- that borrowers give evidence that they have the wheat that is required by the amount of loan for which they apply, and that it is not pledged under section 88 to some other bank.
What was the other problem?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I asked generally about the use of the money and the refusal of the bank on the basis of a proper application.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. The bank has no right to ask what the money is going to be used for. Such information is not required by the government, and although my hon. friend says it is required by the bank, I cannot challenge that statement, but I doubt it. I have received many letters myself from people who expressed surprise

at the ease with which they obtained loans. One said he had never met a bank manager before but was delighted with his reception and with the ease at which the loan was forthcoming. I cannot believe that, if there had been any great resistance in carrying out the spirit of this legislation, I would not have heard about it before directly from the persons concerned.
Then, the hon. member asked if the application for a loan was filed with Ottawa. The applications for loans that are granted are filed with Ottawa, and must be, because Ottawa guarantees each individual loan. I think that answers the question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the minister also indicate the machinery? I am a farmer who goes into a bank and signs an application. Is it still a fact that that application has to be sent to Ottawa for consideraion here? If not, what is the explanation for the delay between the time of the application and the granting of the credit where credit is granted?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Of course, the application is not sent to Ottawa as now suggested. The bank manager must determine whether that same grain has been pledged to another bank. He does that, as I understand it, by telephoning the clearing house at Regina. It should not require much time, and I doubt if it is a matter involving any great time. The bank manager has to make that one search of the title to the grain.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Is there any submission to the Bank of Canada or the officials here?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No, not before the loan is granted. When the loan is reported, it is filed here at Ottawa.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to mention the point about the ease with which an applicant may be able to get a loan. I want to say the information I have received in many instances is contrary to the information or the letters to which the minister referred. I have information that it is very difficult for many applicants to get loans, and for many of them the amount of the loan they are able to obtain is a good deal less than that for which they have applied.
I want to ask the minister about some cases based on information given to me on the way particular applicants were treated. A farmer went into a bank and asked for a loan. He was provided with a loan of $700 on December 20. The minister has said it is not proper for the bank to take any part of the farmer's loan to discharge any other responsibility that the farmer may owe the

bank at that time. As I understood the information the minister gave to the house before, it is not proper for a bank manager to deduct from the amount of money the farmer may obtain under this legislation the amount of money that may be owing the bank at that time under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
In this case at the time the application was made the bank did not attempt to deduct the amount owing under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Here is the way the bank operated according to the information given to me. The farmer was given a loan of $700 on December 20. It was deposited to his account. The farmer came back 11 days later to take the $700 out of his account, but the bank had moved in in the meantime and taken $300 out of it to pay moneys owing under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I am wondering if that practice is proper, and whether the bank had any right to use a back-door method to accomplish something I understand is improper, and perhaps even illegal. When a farmer is making an application, is it within the right of the bank to move in a few days later after the loan has been made and take from the amount the farmer received an amount owing to the bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The action of the bank some days after the loan has been granted is a matter for a lawyer. It has nothing to do with this act. Your correspondent had better discuss it with his lawyer to see whether the bank had a right to go into his account and take $300.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What is the point of having this kind of legislation and having the minister say it is improper for a bank to deduct from the amount of money a farmer can obtain any amount he may owe under another act if the bank, a few days later, can come in and take that money from the farmer's account?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Surely you would not expect the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Trade and Commerce to guard that money for 11 days after it was paid to the farmer. If he had put the money in his pants pocket and walked away, you might as well expect us to protect him from being robbed on his way home.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is a point I should like to raise with reference to one subclause of clause 5. The clause in general permits the governor in council to make regulations, and then paragraph (e) reads:
(e) respecting subrogation of Her Majesty to the rights of a bank with respect to a guaranteed loan.
Grain
As hon. members are aware, the purpose of subrogation is to permit the guarantor or surety, in the event of default, to step into the rights of the person who has put up the loan in the first place. In this case, presumably the intent of the section is to permit regulations to be passed under which Her Majesty will be able to step into the position of the bank in relation to the rights of the bank as against the original borrower.
Now, while the regulations are not technically in existence, nevertheless the whole borrowing scheme is and I would like the minister to indicate what the provisions in regard to subrogation contain in this regard. Would he outline with particularity the procedure that is provided for and contemplated in the event of default? If it is clear that default has been made and the farmer is not in a position to remedy his default, what are the steps then to be taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I can read to my hon. friend the regulation under the 1951 legislation. I assume that the same regulation would apply in this legislation. The regulation reads:
Where payment is made by the Minister of Finance to a bank under the act in respect of any loss sustained by the bank as a result of a guaranteed loan, the bank shall execute a receipt in accordance with form "E" in the schedule to these regulations or a form to the like effect in favour of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce on behalf of His Majesty shall thereupon be subrogated in and to all the rights of the bank in respect of such loan and without limiting the generality of the foregoing, all rights and powers of the bank in respect of the loan, and in respect of any judgment in respect thereof obtained by the bank, and in respect of any security taken by the bank for the repayment thereof shall thereupon be vested in the Minister of Trade and Commerce, on behalf of His Majesty, and that minister shall be entitled on behalf of His Majesty to exercise all the rights, powers and privileges which the bank had or might exercise in respect of such loan, judgment or security, and to commence or continue any action or proceeding in respect thereof, and to execute any documents necessary by way of release, transfer, sale or assignment thereof, or in any way to realize thereon.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that dealt with the first part of my inquiry. The minister has indicated that similar regulations are in contemplation here. There can be no doubt that the regulation he read from the 1951 act provides for complete rights of subrogation so that if similar regulations are passed under the authority of clause 5 we may assume then that Her Majesty will step into all the rights that the banks enjoy under their original contractual relations with the borrower.
This raises the question as to the policy as well as the question as to procedure. I would ask the minister whether he would deal with the second part of my inquiry? Assume that

Grain
the fault has arisen; that the bank has satisfied itself that there cannot be any immediate recovery, and that the borrower is not in a position to remedy his default, put himself in good standing, and the government has been called upon to make good the guarantee. Is it the intention of the government in any such case to insist that the bank should first take judgment, or what process is the government going to insist that the bank take before it will be satisfied to pay under the terms of the guarantee? Assume that the circumstances have arisen under which the government has paid on the guarantee, what is the procedure contemplated and the policy in view on the part of the government with respect to enforcing the rights to which it is subrogated?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the action would depend upon the circumstances of each individual case. I might tell my hon. friend though that in connection with the 1951 legislation there was no case in which judgment was obtained against the borrower.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman,-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: May I just follow that up? May I take it, then, that it is not the intention of the government to insist that the bank shall obtain a judgment and presumably a return of "no goods" on the execution issued under the judgment before it will pay on its guarantee to the bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Well, I am not going to say what the intention would be. I do not know what the circumstances will be. All I can say is, it is a matter of record that loans were defaulted under the 1951 legislation and no judgment against the debtor was obtained.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: And the government made good its guarantee without insisting on a judgment being taken? Is that the minister's answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was somewhat puzzled by the reply the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave to the hon. member for Assiniboia. I was wondering whether the Minister of Finance would agree with the minister's statement. I gather from what the minister said that if a farmer owed the bank money and then borrowed from the bank under this legislation, the only safe thing for him to do would be to draw that money out of the bank in currency, put it in his pocket and walk away with it; otherwise, there would be nothing to stop the bank from raiding that farmer's account and taking out the money he has in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I said nothing of the sort. The hon. member for Assiniboia was mentioning what had happened to cash deposited in the bank eleven days after the deposit had been made. My point was that the government's responsibility is no different then from what it would have been had the farmer, instead of depositing it in the bank, put it in his pocket and walked away with it. Eleven days earlier the government had passed out of the picture. The money passed out of the jurisdiction of the government when the loan was made and the money paid over.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The only safe way is for the farmer to take out in currency the money that he borrows and take it away with him because-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I suggest that is your statement, not mine. I made no statement that can be twisted or turned into that statement.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You said that eleven days later the bank might consider raiding the account. The logical thing for the farmer borrowing from a bank to do would be to deposit it in the bank. Then he could issue cheques against that. It might take eleven days for those cheques to come back to the bank, and by the time the cheques came back his account might be marked N.S.F. because the bank had in the meantime raided the account. That is a very unsatisfactory situation. There should be some understanding with the farmer. If this legislation is being passed for a specific purpose, then the bank has no right to seize the money when it is deposited.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I have only the word of the hon. member for Assiniboia on that point.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I have the evidence in my hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Why not give it to a competent lawyer in your district and have him take action?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is not the point. It should not be necessary for a farmer to have to go to the expense of hiring a lawyer to safeguard himself under this legislation. I should like to have an interpretation of the situation from the Minister of Finance. Does he think it is ethical for a bank to raid the account of a farmer when money is deposited under this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think we ought to be too much concerned about an isolated case. One does not know precisely what the situation may have been. As everyone knows, when a customer in indebted to a bank he may very well sign an authority

to the bank under which the bank may at any time take some sums of money for the purpose of adjusting accounts. In this particular case I have no doubt whatever that the hon. member for Assiniboia is correctly reporting what he has been advised. But let us suppose that at the time the borrower said to the bank manager: Now, I am going to have to spend about $500 to pay this and this, and when I get through with that I may have no other debts. But I want $900 now to be sure I have more than enough. We cannot be sure that there was not a tacit understanding that at some time if there was a surplus in the account the bank manager might take it by agreement or understanding.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may we have some understanding of this from the Minister of Justice? The hon. member for Acadia asked a very important question. It is a legal question. The minister pointed out a particular case. I can understand that in a particular case, such as the instance given, the borrower may have given the bank the right to take certain moneys from his account and apply them on a bill owing to the bank. But generally speaking, we should have a statement from the Minister of Justice telling us whether the banks have the right to take money from an account, money which has been obtained under this legislation, and then make deductions from the farmer's account in order to offset it against that which he owes to the bank without authority from that individual farmer in that particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, excuse me if I answer before the Minister of Justice. The whole purpose of the legislation is to assure to the farmer the maximum amount of the loan. It has been understood that the banks will not take from the loan the amount of their indebtedness in other respects. Now, if it happens that a bank manager has done this, and if there has not been an understanding between them, I shall be glad to communicate with the bank concerned, because the purpose of the legislation is to give additional ready money to the farmer. I do not think we need a legal opinion; all we need is the persuasion of public opinion and the desire of parliament.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the minister for the remarks he has just made. I do not see anything wrong with the bank suggesting to the farmer that part of that money might be used to make a payment under the Farm Improvement Loans Act but it seems to me it should be done by agreement at the time the loan is made.
Grain

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister a question with regard to paragraph (f). What is the form and purpose in which it is envisaged the reports of the banks to the Canadian wheat board will be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Before a new permit book can be issued it is necessary for the wheat board to know what loans are outstanding against the book which is being replaced. The reference has to do with the endorsement of the permit book.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: As I understand it, then, the sole purpose of this paragraph concerns the issuing of new permit books. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: And that is the only reason for a report to the wheat board at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 7-Effect of endorsement.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Clause 7 (a) provides that no manager or operator of an elevator shall, after the coming into force of this act, receive for storage grain delivered by or on behalf of the borrower who made the endorsement.
It is found that while that provision was contained in the 1951 legislation it is not required in this legislation and I would ask my colleague the Minister of Finance to move:
That clause 7 of Bill No. 82 be amended by deleting paragraph (a) therefrom and relettering paragraphs (b) and (c) respectively as (a) and (b).

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
That of course removes an obvious anomaly in this section. However, I should like to draw the remainder of the clause to the attention of the committee. The part I refer to is this. If the manager of an elevator, or in other words the local buyer or any other person, receives delivery of grain, then that person becomes personally liable by action or proceedings for the recovery of the amount owing to the bank to the extent of the value of the crop that was delivered to the elevator buyer or manager.
There was a similar section in the old act. I should like to ask the minister what was the experience in the 1951 act in relation to the whole of clause 7. Were there any actions taken to the knowledge of the minister or his officials under this clause? I would think this imposes a very heavy onus on the buyer, the elevator operator or manager of the local elevator. It may be that it is just one of those clauses that has been borrowed holus-bolus out of the old act and stuck into this one, if I may use that expression.

Grain
But if it were actually enforced it imposes a heavy liability on the local buyer and one which few buyers would be willing to undertake.
Would the minister let the committee know the experience under the old act, because I personally know of no action taken under the old act and I wonder whether or not there were any such actions taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my responsible officer tells me that under the old act there were no cases where the money was not collected and turned over to the bank as provided in the legislation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It would appear to me there should be an additional amendment in paragraph (c). Reference is made there to paragraph (b). I imagine the minister would want to move another amendment. Where the letter (b) appears in line 26 of paragraph (c) it should be changed to (a).

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: That is correct. Thank you for the correction. I am just having the amendment written out. We discovered it at about the same time my hon. friend discovered it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Two good lawyers.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.
