maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: In the meantime, would it be the wish of the committee to pass the first amendment? Is the amendment already moved by Mr. Garson agreed to?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
A further
amendment, which is really part of the same amendment, is moved as follows:
That in new paragraph (b) the words "paragraph (b)" in line 26 be amended to be "paragraph (a)".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think the committee has heard the motion made by Mr. Garson. Is this amendment agreed to?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before we leave clause 7 I wish to refer again to what is now paragraph (b) with the amendment which refers to the responsibility of the manager of the elevator with respect to the bank taking proceedings to collect. I should like to know whether that means the person responsible as manager of the elevator, the person who at that time happens to be the manager, or what we call an elevator agent, or whether it could also refer to any person succeeding him in that job who assumes that responsibility.

For example, at the time a loan was granted there may be one particular person who is the agent of a particular elevator. He gets moved, let us say, 30 days later before the loan is paid back. Does the new agent who replaces him assume the same responsibility that is placed upon the current agent by this act?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The man responsible would be the man who accepted the wheat and endorsed the permit book knowing that there was a claim registered in the permit book against that particular grain. It would be the operator at the time the grain was accepted for delivery.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Regardless of whether that particular agent happens to be still an agent of the company by which he is employed, and regardless of the fact that he may have moved away entirely and taken on other employment, he still carries on that responsibility as an individual. Is that the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He had no responsibility. He made no loan. The loan was made by the bank. The only responsibility on the agent is that when grain is presented for delivery on a permit book against which is endorsed an undischarged loan, it is the duty of the elevator agent to make out two tickets, one for the farmer and the other for the bank.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can hardly agree with the minister when he puts it that way. I will read the words in the paragraph that are pertinent to the question: the bank in whose favour the endorsement was made may recover any of the moneys to which it is entitled under paragraph (b) -
-which now reads paragraph (a); and these are the words'-
by action or proceedings against the manager of the elevator or other person receiving delivery of the grain or receiving such moneys-
The responsibility of the agent or the manager of the elevator does not cease when he has issued the duplicate ticket. The bank may take action or proceedings against him. It must be remembered that clause 7 begins with these words:
Notwithstanding any other act or law-
That means that this legislation supersedes any other act or law and is a law unto itself. I can hardly agree with the minister that when a responsible agent issues a duplicate ticket on the delivery of grain he should be faced with the possibility of having action or proceedings taken against him. How long will he have to face the possibility of a bank taking proceedings against him even though

Grain
he may be no longer employed by the elevator company on whose behalf he purchased the grain? Does that go on indefinitely or is there any limitation?

Every person who. after the coming into force of this act, in respect of a guaranteed loan
(a)	knowingly makes any misrepresentation in any application or other document or wilfully furnishes any false or misleading information; or

(3) When a person is convicted of an offence under this section, there shall be imposed on him, in addition to any fine, a penalty equal to the amount of the guaranteed loan that has not been repaid by him together with interest on the loan to the date of payment of the penalty-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Paragraph (a) of clause 9 reads:
knowingly makes any misrepresentation in any application or other document or wilfully furnishes any false or misleading information;
It is a practice in western Canada to do a large part of harvesting with combines and I am sure that there is no farmer who could estimate accurately the amount of grain he has in his granary. Therefore I am sure that 99 farmers out of 100 will be providing false information as to the quantity they have on hand. Subclause 2 reads:
A prosecution under subsection (1) may be instituted at any time within two years from the time when the subject matter of the complaint arose.
Then paragraph (b) reads:
If he is a borrower and his loan has not been repaid in full, delivers, or causes any other person to deliver on his behalf, under a permit book that has not been endorsed by the borrower as required by this act, any grain of which he is the actual producer,
is guilty of an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars.
Section 694 of the Criminal Code reads:
(1)	Except where otherwise expressly provided by law, every one who is convicted of an offence punishable on summary conviction is liable to a fine of not more than five hundred dollars or to imprisonment for six months or to both.
(2)	Where the imposition of a fine or the making of an order for the payment of money is authorized by law, but the law does not provide that imprisonment may be imposed in default of payment of the fine or compliance with the order, the court may order that in default of payment of the fine or compliance with the order, as the case may be, the defendant shall be imprisoned for a period of not more than six months.
(3)	A summary conviction court may direct that any fine, pecuniary penalty or sum of money adjudged to be paid shall be paid forthwith or, if the accused is unable to pay forthwith, at such time and on such terms as the summary conviction court may fix.
The people who are going to be affected by this legislation are short of cash although they may have plenty of grain. Certainly it would not be difficult to establish that a farmer has given information not in accordance with the facts, and a penalty of $500 would seem to be

Grain
heavy under circumstances where the maximum amount he can borrow is $1,500. If a farmer cannot put his hands on the cash and must go to jail for six months it would seem a most objectionable provision. I feel sure that, when farmers are confronted with this possibility, even a smaller percentage will apply for loans than applied in 1951. I wish the minister would consider reviewing this section so that the penalty would not involve a farmer going to jail if he found himself in the position where he could not market any grain for cash and had nothing with which to pay his fine except grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the fact that the section in question has received the approval of an hon. member who, I think we will all agree, is one of the most eminent criminal lawyers in Canada, the hon. member for Prince Albert, should indicate that there is not very much wrong with it from the standpoint of the accused. Otherwise the hon. member for Prince Albert would not have approved it.
I might say for the benefit of my hon. friend from Mackenzie that in drafting a bill of the sort that we now have under consideration the draftsman has to take into account the existing body of the law. Although it may seem to my hon. friend that this clause creates an offence which he may have thought did not exist before, actually the effect of this clause is to change this stated set of facts which would otherwise constitute the offence under the Criminal Code, of obtaining credit by false pretences, which would be triable upon indictment and carry a maximum penalty of ten years. Having regard to the fact that the offence contemplated here is of a less serious character -than the usual offence of obtaining credit by false pretences, it has been set up in the form of what in effect is an amendment to the code. This bill provides that any misrepresentations under clause 9 (1) (a) shall be an offence triable upon summary conviction, for which the penalty shall be a fine not exceeding $500. I think my hon. friend from Mackenzie will agree that this is a very much lesser maximum penalty than ten years' imprisonment. That being the case, the effect of this present provision, as I have said, is to reduce very greatly the character of the offence and the nature of the punishment from what they would be under existing law.
After the accused has been found guilty- not, as my hon. friend has suggested, of merely conveying wrong information, but of knowingly making any misrepresentations in any application or other document or of wilfully furnishing any false or misleading information-he would be punished much more lightly and, we think, much more fairly,

in relation to the kind of case that my hon. friend from Mackenzie has just suggested, than he would be if we were to have left the law as it would have been but for the passage of this clause.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, will the Minister of Justice agree with me that any farmer who has a granary full of grain will admit very frankly that when he says he has 1,200 bushels in the granary, that is misleading, and it might be 1,100 or 1,300 bushels?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think at some point later he will be forced to admit that it is misleading information as to the exact amount of grain he has. I think the Minister of Justice could come out with some sort of wording that would be less offensive and some way of imposing penalties that would be less severe than we have in this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
With all deference to my hon. friend, I would suggest to him that the language that has been proven by experience, not over years but over decades, in the Criminal Code is the language that is indicated here: knowingly and wilfully making false representations.
Let us consider the case of which my hon. friend speaks, where a farmer, not being too sure about the quantity of grain in his bin, was inaccurate, but unintentionally so, in making his application for a loan. If any prosecution were later to be based upon that set of facts, the Crown would have to prove beyond all reasonable doubt-and the accused would be entitled to the benefit of the doubt- that not only was the information incorrect but that the accused gave that incorrect information wilfully and knowingly with the intention of securing credit to which he was not lawfully entitled.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on July 31, 1955, there were in store, over the 178 million bushels which is considered normal, another 217 million bushels of wheat, and that 217 million bushels of wheat is the wheat referred as coming under this guarantee. All that wheat belonged to the 1954-55 pool. However, the amount belonging to the pool diminishes day by day as sales and deliveries for export are made. The wheat board receives the government's payments each month, applying on the grain in store.
To the extent that the grain in store is grain from the 1954-55 pool, it will apply to that pool. To the extent that the 1954-55 grain has been disposed of and replaced by grain in the 1955-56 pool the payment will apply to that grain. It is just a matter of bookkeeping for the wheat board to determine to which pool the payments are to be apportioned. This will be done month by month. It is customary to transfer the remainder of one pool into the next pool when a considerable proportion of the pool has been sold and priced. We have never, I think, transferred as much as 100 million bushels from one pool to the other.
Just when the transfer can take place, I do not know. We receive a recommendation from the wheat board when the proper time comes, and at that time the cabinet decides whether it can accept the recommendation

Wheat
of the wheat board. In this case the situation is somewhat complicated by the fact that when we discovered there was a filibuster under way here we decided we could not ask the producer to wait. Therefore we authorized an interim payment instead of the final payment.
Obviously the amount of the final payment could not be determined until this bill had either been passed or rejected. Now that it has been passed we will continue with the interim payment, and in due course the government will decide to accept the recommendation of the wheat board and the final payment on the 1954-55 pool will be made. After that decision has been arrived at we will be able to announce it in the house.

speechtext:
The statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the passage of this bill was held up by the debate on Bill No. 82 is not accurate at all. The fact that this bill has been delayed until this day is because the government has held back in calling this bill when announcing the business of the house. We in the C.C.F. group and all members of the opposition have been ready from the moment parliament assembled to pass this legislation with a minimum of delay. Nothing the Minister of Trade and Commerce can say can show that we have not been prepared at all times to pass this legislation since it was announced to the house.
As a matter of fact we did our best by way of a vote to get the government to alter its order of business. The fact that this measure has been delayed so long is not only because the leader of the house from time to time announced Bill No. 82 ahead of Bill No. 83, but because the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself on February 3 moved a motion to reverse the decision the house had taken earlier, namely to proceed with the resolution preceding the bill now under discussion. The minister's excuse cannot stand up at all. The government does what it wants so far as announcing the business of the house is concerned.
It' is the governor in council who decides when an interim payment will be made or *when a final payment will be made. I suggest to the minister that a combined interim and final payment on the 1954-55 wheat pool should be made immediately. The minister has said there is a good deal of wheat still in that account. This should not make any difference. The wheat board and the minister know the price at which grain is being sold today. We have the assurance of the minister, repeated time after time, that grain is being sold now in very large quantities. He says there is no doubt about it; it is all going to be sold in a very short time. I do not see any reason why western producers should have to wait for several weeks, perhaps many months, before they receive a final payment. We have had far too much jockeying in the past by the government with the dates of interim and final payments. I suggest the government should be prepared at a given date following each crop year to make a final payment, and at a given date during the crop year to announce an interim payment.
There is another disadvantage to making an interim payment at this time and a final payment at a later time rather than making a combined payment right now. It.is the additional cost. It costs a substantial sum of money to make thousands of cheques payable to producers, and the producers themselves

Wheat
have to pay the cost of making that extra payment. The final payment, if it were announced now, would be about one year late so far as our experience in the past is concerned. I suggest that the government has erred in not announcing, instead of a small interim payment, a larger final payment so that the account could be closed.

It is unfortunate, however, that a calamity in Europe is going to be responsible for a great many of those countries being short of grain. This points up the value of having in the world stocks of food for emergencies.
I think it is only right and proper that all the people of Canada should carry some part of the cost of maintaining those stocks. I am very glad that no one in the house, with the exception of the hon. member for Vancouver Burrard, has offered any objections to this legislation.

speechtext:
Before this clause carries I would like to get some information. Some time ago I asked the government a question regarding elevator space. When I received the answer I was amazed at the amount of empty space in terminal elevators. I want to know why that situation exists. Is it because of a shortage of box cars or not? Before the minister answers I have another problem to put to him. There was an editorial in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix around February 17 which said this:
Transport controller Roy W. Milner, whose powers parliament will be asked to renew for two years, said Thursday there is no shortage of box cars holding up prairie grain shipments.
In the same article we find the following:
Meanwhile, Jake Schulz of Winnipeg head of the interprovincial farm union council, said he is confused by Mr. Milner's remarks. The council is made up of farm groups in the prairie provinces, Ontario and British Columbia.
In a brief before the cabinet, the council had attacked the transport controller because of a reported box car shortage, saying it shows Mr. Milner "is failing in his duties and thus betraying the trust of the farmers".
Mr. Schulz said later he brought up the matter during the council's meeting with the cabinet and was informed by trade minister Howe that because

of a box car shortage, prairie grain elevators will not be emptied before the spring navigation season opens.
"What are we to believe?" he asked.
Mr. Howe, under opposition fire because of federal grain policies, recently said in the commons that the big problem in selling wheat was not markets but transportation.
There is a confusion of opinion there. Later on in the same article we find the following:
Mr. Marler, speaking at Saint John, New Brunswick, Wednesday said figures he has received this month "give me good reason to be confident that the railways are doing an excellent job."
Some critics have suggested that the government's decision to pay storage charges on abnormal wheat carryovers in the hands of the wheat board is complicating the issue.
The government has conceded there is room in elevators for more grain. But the more wheat that is packed into the elevators, the higher the charges the treasury will have to bear, unless the wheat is sold.
What I want to know is, why has this space been accumulating in terminal elevators? Is it going to be the policy of the government to back up the grain on the farms and keep the terminal elevators with a lot of empty space?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: I may say that I am confused after listening to my hon. friend. The purpose of the government is to move grain from the farms just as rapidly as possible. There is a very great demand for wheat at the ocean shipping ports, particularly at Vancouver, Halifax and Saint John. The weather conditions in western Canada have been very bad indeed. A combination of circumstances has not made it possible to deliver the required grain at export points and at the same time fill elevator space within Canada. An effort is being made to do both, and I think the situation is improving from day to day. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not satisfied yet. The minister himself spoke in Edmonton in November. maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
After my hon. friend listens to the evidence given in the

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: The title of this bill is the temporary wheat reserves act. Presumably we are to enact it as a temporary measure. It is fair then to ask the minister what is his best estimate of the length of time over which this measure is likely to be in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: I could not give an estimate unless my hon. friend is prepared to tell me what is his estimate of the size of next year's crop, and what will be conditions generally. This is self-liquidating legislation. It stays in force until the carryover at the end of any crop year is less than 178 million bushels.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: I am going to ask the minister a straight question. Is there a shortage of box cars in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: That is a matter of opinion. I am not prepared to express my opinion. I expressed an opinion at Edmonton in the speech to which the hon. member referred. He can take one opinion; I will take another. As I say, he can get the opinions all collected in one room. He will have to make up his mind then.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:

If at the commencement of a crop year the stocks of wheat of the board are not in excess of 178 million bushels, no payment shall be made by the Minister of Finance to the board under this act in respect of that or any subsequent crop year.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: That is the liquidating clause. It means that if at the 1st day of August in any year the carryover does not amount to 178 million bushels, this act becomes a dead letter.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I take it that might quite easily mean one bushel stored away some place. The act could be carried on for another year if one extra bushel had to be carried over. If that is the correct meaning of it, that is the situation.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
What of it?
Wheat

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES

One bushel on the 1st day of
August.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: By the same token, it would seem rather strange if on the 30th day of September, for instance, after the harvest, there was a carryover in excess of 178 million bushels, probably 200 million bushels, then you do not pay the storage on that for the whole of that crop year?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: That is not carryover. If my hon. friend would pay a little more attention in the committees that he attends every year he would know that carryover is the amount of grain in store at the end of the crop year, which occurs on the 31st day of July in every year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:

Wheat

speechtext:
I wonder if the minister could give us some idea of the policy that will likely be followed, let us say during the latter half of a crop year before we arrive at August 1. on the farms. The amount for which payment would be made would be reduced by 58 million bushels. I am wondering if the minister could say what general policy will be followed toward the end of the crop year so this legislation may be as effective as I believe it is intended to be.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as to what grain the wheat board buys, I might say it buys any grain the farmer wishes to deliver on his permit book. maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: As far as shipments are concerned it is always the purpose of everyone connected with wheat to get the wheat as far forward as possible as transportation may make possible. We might have a shipping strike on the great lakes which would intervene, but generally speaking an attempt is made to fill the elevators at the seaports and fill the elevators supporting the ports so there will be reserves against all shipping delays. To do that we make space in the country, and of course farmers wish to deliver wheat to fill that space. I do not think the difficulty foreseen by my hon. friend is likely to arise as a problem if there is a surplus of wheat in the country.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: I am extremely pleased to obtain that assurance from the minister. I do not want anything I have said to be taken as a reflection on either the minister, the wheat board or the policies they follow. I may just express the hope that box cars will be available so that the large amount of space now available will be filled by July 31.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister what is the purpose of the monthly instalments instead of paying this as a lump sum at the end of the year, when the amount of the carryover is determined?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: We have been asked to consider a winding up of the 1954-55 pool. Unless the money is in hand it will be difficult to wind up the pool. The purpose of paying monthly is that storage charges are usually paid monthly, and the government should properly pay monthly storage charges on grain the government itself is carrying.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: As I understand it, the carryover at the end of the crop year is determined and on anything in excess of 178 million bushels the government is going to pay storage charges. That amount is determined right there and then, as far as I can make out; is that not the intent and purpose of the act? I am therefore just wondering why these payments will be made monthly instead of being made there and then. Is not the matter determined at that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: Is it my hon. friend's suggestion that it be prepaid? The amount of the payment for the succeeding year is determined on August 31, but the charges do not accrue until the storage has been used. maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: No.

speechtext: Why does the minister say no? Is the amount on which storage is going to be paid to vary from month to month throughout the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: No, the amount paid is on the carryover at the end of the crop year, so many bushels. This year the amount is 217 million bushels. Under this bill that 217 million bushels is to be carried throughout the crop year, no more, no less. That will be the case every year. We carry a definite amount as prescribed in this bill.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Surely the minister is not saying that the board is going to carry 217 million bushels plus 178 million bushels throughout the year. If they can find customers for it they are going to sell it. That is the point I am raising, that the amount of the 67509-98J

payment is going to be determined at the end of the crop year and paid in monthly instalments throughout the year, instead of in a lump sum when the determination is made.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES

million bushels in excess in storage as of August 1, would you pay the storage costs on those 200 million bushels for the entire year?

No, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps I could explain it this way. We have always been asked to set up a government reserve of wheat, and that is really what this bill does. How do we fix the amount of the reserve? We fix it by the carryover at the end of the crop year on July 31. If that carryover is 178 million bushels, which is normal, plus 217 million bushels, which was the case last July, that 217 million bushels is taken as the reserve which the government will carry for that year. My hon. friend will say that we will be shipping out of that reserve and replacing it, which would mean that it would not be the identical wheat, but we would be taking on 217 million bushels this year as a reserve which the government will carry in the national interest. My hon. friend can argue up and down but that is the situation.	.

eastern Canada will become much more disturbed knowing that that is the fact. Who is going to get that six months' storage? The government is going to pay out money when in fact the wheat was not in storage at the time it was paid for.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: July 31 is the period between the two crops. That is when the old crop would normally be shipped out and before the new crop starts to move. maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES

IMr. Howe (Port Arthur).]
board is going to have on hand at any time in the year will be about August 1, before the new crop is harvested. maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
As far as I can see the minister has not yet answered my question as to why this should not be paid in a lump sum. He said, "Do you want us to prepay it?" It is not a matter of prepaying it at all. Some of it may have been in the elevator for a year and a half, and certainly the wheat would be in for varying lengths of time. In any event the wheat board will have already paid the storage charges on the wheat and under this bill the money is going to be paid by the government at the rates laid down. The thing I cannot see is why that payment is not made at the end of the crop year when the amount that is going to be paid is determined, instead of being made as provided by this subsection in twelve monthly instalments. period must have been in the other pool, because the grain delivered in 1954-55 belongs to the 1954-55 pool. Those charges accumulate daily, but they are settled on a monthly basis. So on the 1st of September we owed certain money; on the 1st of October we owed certain money; and on the 1st of November we owed certain money. We have not been able to pay that money because we did not have the legislation, but we are going to settle our debt in a lump sum to the end of February. speechtext: Then may I ask the minister this question. This is the situation, as I understand it. This money that is going to be paid, in this case about $32 million, I think the minister said, is going to be available to settle up the 1954-55 bills, is it not?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES

in the old pool is a diminishing amount until the old pool is wholly disposed of, and he will see that the amount payable on the 1955-56 pool is an accelerating amount until all the wheat for which we are responsible is wheat belonging to the 1955-56 pool.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: No.

speechtext: That is certainly what is being done as far as the present situation is concerned. CHURCH OF ENGLAND IN CANADA
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 122, an act respecting the general synod of the Church of England in Canada, the missionary society of the Church of England in Canada, the women's auxiliary of the Church of England in Canada and the Church of England consolidated trust fund.
He said: In order to understand the purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary to know something about the organization and administration of the Anglican Church of Canada. For purposes of church government the fundamental unit of the Anglican Church of Canada is the diocese, which is under the authority and guidance of a bishop in matters both spiritual and temporal. The diocese of Newfoundland to which I belong was founded in 1839 with the Right Rev. Aubrey George Spencer as its first bishop. Previous to this Newfoundland had been administered as part of the diocese of Nova Scotia, which had been founded in 1787. In 1844 Bishop Spencer was succeeded by Bishop Field.
The letters patent which nominated the Rev. Edward Field as bishop also declared that on appointment Bishop Field would become a body corporate with the ordinary powers and functions of any corporate body. As soon as a diocese is sufficiently well organized a governing body known as the diocesan synod is set up to administer the temporal affairs of the diocese.
The diocesan synod of Newfoundland was organized in 1870 and incorporated in 1875. Every diocesan synod is composed of two houses, the house of the clergy which includes all the clergy active in the diocese,

and the house of the laity which is composed of the lay delegates appointed by each parish at its annual meeting. Matters which affect the whole church of Canada are in the hands of a corporate body now known as the general synod of the Anglican Church of Canada. This general synod is composed of two houses, the upper house or the house of bishops and the lower house made up of a body of lay and clerical delegates who are elected in equal numbers by each synod. It will be seen, therefore, that the system of government employed by the Anglican Church of Canada closely parallels our own federal system. The diocesan synod would be the counterpart of the provincial government and the general synod would be the counterpart of our own parliament of Canada.
The last meeting of the general synod took place at Edmonton, Alberta, from August 30 to September 8 of last year. The upper house consisted of 40 bishops, of whom 28 were diocesan bishops and the remainder were retired bishops. The lower house was composed of 284 elected delegates, half of whom were lay delegates and half clerical. One of the first matters considered by the general synod at this last meeting at Edmonton to which I have just referred was the following resolution:
Resolved that the church hitherto known as the Church of England in Canada shall in future be styled the Anglican Church of Canada.
After due consideration and debate this resolution was passed by both houses with a substantial majority. The vote in the upper house or the house of bishops was 23 to 4 and in the lower house 174 to 40. I should like to make it quite clear that the decision of the general synod to change the name of the church requires no parliamentary sanction whatever. However, at various times in the past this parliament of Canada has passed a number of acts dealing with various bodies and organizations affiliated with the church and with the property owned by those bodies. As the name of the church has been written into some of these acts, the purpose of this bill is to effect a corresponding change in the name of the church wherever it appears in any of these measures.
Hon. members may wish to know why it was decided that a change of name was necessary. I can assure hon. members that it was not a snap decision. It has been under consideration on and off for over 40 years. It first came before the general synod in 1911. It was considered by the general synods of 1915, 1918 and 1921. It came up again in 1931 and was dropped until 1949. While support 67509-99
Private Bills
for the change tended to increase during the years, on none of those occasions was there sufficient support to have the change approved by any of the general synods. In 1954 the Primate set up a commission to study the whole matter, and it was the recommendation of this commission, embodied in the form of a resolution, that was passed at the last general synod.
The primary reason for the change was that the name "Church of England in Canada" no longer properly describes the present autonomous and independent status of the church in Canada as it did in the early days of its history.
Hon. members may recall I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks that the diocese of Newfoundland was founded in 1839. Prior to that date the work of the church in Newfoundland, and in all the colonies, was financed from the mother church in England and carried out under the direction and authority of the Bishop of London. The first chaplain arrived in Newfoundland from England in 1583, and it is possible that this date may mark the beginning of the history of the Anglican Church of Canada.
The cathedral parish of St. John's, Newfoundland, of which I am a member, claims the distinction of being the oldest parish of the Anglican church in Canada. It was organized by Rev. John Jackson in 1699, and financed largely by funds supplied by church organizations in the old country. One of these organizations was the society for the promotion of Christian knowledge, commonly known as S.P.C.K.; another was the S.P.G., or the society for the propagation of the gospel.
Today the situation is quite different. The Anglican Church of Canada is financially independent and conducts its own missionary activities in various parts of the world. Indeed, one of the highlights of the general synod at Edmonton was the presentation of a gift of $50,000 to the newly-appointed Bishop of Korea for his work in that diocese. No longer do our clergy come to us from England. Our clergy today are recruited from our own congregations and trained in our own Canadian theological colleges. Our bishops are no longer nominated by letters patent. They are now elected by the diocese which they are called upon to govern. It is quite probable that the late Bishop of Newfoundland, the Right Rev. Philip Abraham, who passed away on December 22, 1955, is the last member of the house of bishops to be consecrated following letters patent.
Another reason was that the missionaries and clergy working among newly arrived immigrants found that the name "Church of

Private Bills
England in Canada" conveyed to these people the erroneous idea that membership in the church was confined and restricted to people of English birth and ancestry. Be that as it may, after many years of consideration this decision to change the name of the church has been approved by a substantial majority in both houses of the general synod. This bill results from that action, and since it is a matter of importance to some 2 million Anglicans in all parts of Canada, I strongly recommend it to the house for approval.

maintopic: CHURCH OF ENGLAND IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to support what my colleague from Burin-Burgeo has said. My words will be few. I think it has been found by the Anglican church in Canada that as Canada has grown and become sovereign in her own right-and particularly is that so since the union with Newfoundland-the church has found herself somewhat in the same position. It is now by this legislation and by law becoming sovereign in its own right in Canada. It is felt that since this nation has grown up and become independent, so the Anglican church in Canada is now Eully grown, and this is another step to show (hat it is now sovereign in its own right. I have much pleasure in supporting the petition of my colleague from Burin-Burgeo.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off).
He said: I confess that it is a temptation to respond to the challenge that was thrown to me a few moments ago by the Minister of Finance, but I also confess that it is not my intention to speak for 45 minutes if for no other reason than that the rules would limit me to 40 minutes. However, I shall limit myself to an even shorter period of time.
The bill now before the house is one which should be well known to all hon. members. It calls for the addition of a subsection to the appropriate section of the labour code, otherwise known as the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which would write into the labour code the voluntary revocable check-off.
The voluntary revocable check-off, Mr. Speaker, is a device whereby the collection of union dues is facilitated particularly in cases where a union has been properly certified and is the recognized bargaining agent in relationships between a group of employees and their employer.
This bill has been before the house a great many times. The history of the way in which the house has dealt with it is, I believe, pretty well known to hon. members. Despite the fact that it has been defeated a number of times some of us still hope that one of these days the government will realize that the rights of labour, one of which is set out in this legislation, deserve the passing of this bill.
As hon. members know, as long ago as 1948 a provision in exactly the words that are spelled out in Bill No. 5 was written into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act when that legislation was before the committee on industrial relations. The sponsor of the motion on the basis of which the check-off was written into the labour code at that time was the then Liberal member for Spadina who is now an hon. member of the other place.
Despite the fact that the committee on industrial relations approved of the check-off

Industrial Relations
being written into the labour code at the time we dealt with it in 1948, when that bill came back to the committee oi the whole house it was opposed by the then minister of labour and on the motion of another private Liberal member it was deleted from the labour code. Ever since then we on this side of the house have been trying to persuade the Liberals to accept this Liberal idea which, as I say, originated so far as legislating efforts in parliament are concerned with the hon. member who is now known as Senator David Croll.
I remind hon. members also that later in that same year the last national convention of the Liberal party was held. National conventions of the Liberal party are historic events; they do not occur very often. There was one in 1919, another was held in 1948 and there is a certain amount of interest as to when the next one will come. At any rate, at the national Liberal convention in 1948 a resolution was passed in support of union security.
Union security is a broad term. It is something which can be implemented in a number of different ways and to varying degrees. It is recognized that the voluntary revocable check-off is one form of union security. Therefore I suggest that the fact that in the spring of 1948 a Liberal member tried to write the voluntary revocable checkoff into the labour code, taken with the fact that the national Liberal federation a few months later passed a resolution supporting union security, is a pretty clear recognition that the rank and file of the Liberal party were in support of the proposal made by the then Liberal member for Spadina.
Despite the fact that the Liberal party .s committed to supporting the principle of anion security, despite the fact that quite a number of Liberal members have voted for this bill across the years-in one session I think the number of Liberals who supported it got as high as 17, which is quite remarkable-the government as a whole has not seen fit to agree to this legislation. I hope the day will come when the government .will see the wisdom of this legislation and will realize that it does involve a recognition of the rights of labour which labour in Canada deserves.
In addition to the support of this principle which has been shown by the Liberal party in the way I have indicated, my bill has had the support of the three groups on this side of the house every time it has come to a vote.
I might point out also that in at least six provinces of Canada the provincial labour legislation includes1 some version of the voluntary revocable check-off. Those provinces are
fMr. Knowles.]
the three in the far west, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, together with three of the maritime provinces, namely Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia.

I was afraid I was going to have an argument over my statement about the check-off, but I am happy to make the correction that Newfoundland regards itself as one of the Atlantic provinces, not as one of the maritime provinces. At any rate, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia of the Atlantic provinces do have the check-off in their labour legislation.
This business of six provinces supporting something has become a bit of a watchword in relation to another piece of legislation. I hope the fact that we have six provinces supporting the principle of the voluntary revocable check-off will make this bill more acceptable to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and to the government in general.
In addition to the six provinces I have mentioned as having the voluntary revocable check-off, I believe that in the minister's own province of New Brunswick there is a provision for the voluntary revocable checkoff with respect to workers in the mines. I do not think the provision in New Brunswick is as broad as it is in the other provinces, but at least there is a partial provision there. In other words we have got beyond this magical number of six, we have got to the point where about six and a half out of the ten provinces have the voluntary revocable check-off.

maintopic: INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
I seem to be having trouble with my friends from the Atlantic and maritime provinces. I hope they will understand that any error is quite unintentional. I did not mean that New Brunswick was half a province, not at all. Perhaps I can put myself in the clear by pointing out that my father was born in Nova Scotia and my mother was born in New Brunswick, so I would not indulge in anything derogatory to the maritime or Atlantic provinces. What I meant was that New Brunswick is half way along with this particular type of legislation.
In addition to the support of this principle which I suggest is indicated by the facts I have stated to date, I am sure the Minister of Labour knows that when the question of the

check-off has come before conciliation boards, more often than not such boards have recommended in favour of some form of union security, and more often than not in favour of the voluntary revocable check-off except in those cases where something better has been recommended such as the Rand formula. It is a few years now since there was a treatise on this matter in one of the issues of the Labour Gazette. However, in that treatise, figures were given showing that out of 125 cases that had pome before conciliation boards where the question of union security was involved, 90 of the boards had recommended in favour of some form of union security.
While across the years the trade union movement has had to fight pretty hard to be recognized-it is a long story and I shall not attempt to go into it at this time-the point has been reached in Canada where it is becoming fairly generally recognized that labour unions are here to stay. They have a tremendously important part to play, not only on their own behalf and on behalf of their members but in the economy of the country, and all possible steps should be taken to accord them full recognition.
Because this point of progress has been reached, to me, to many of us on this side of the house, and I think to quite a few on the Liberal side of the house as well, it is disappointing that the federal government is still dragging its feet so far as this matter is concerned. It may be pointed out, and quite successfully, that a good many of the employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction already have the check-off in one form or another. For example, the railway employees have even more than the voluntary revocable check-off; they have the Rand formula.
Surely with this principle being established by law in so many other jurisdictions the time has come when the federal government-it can no longer give the lead because that has been taken by others-should follow along and put this principle into our federal labour legislation.
As to the meaning of the phrase, voluntary revocable check-off, I believe this is pretty well covered by the language of the bill. I do not think the wording is ambiguous as the drafting of bills sometimes is. May I spell it out by saying that what is involved in the voluntary revocable check-off is that when a union has been certified by the Canada labour relations board as the bargaining agent for a group of employees, then and only then that union has the right to request, which request must be granted, a check-off
Industrial Relations
of the dues of its members. Even after that, under the terms of the voluntary revocable formula, the dues of individual members are checked off, that is deducted from the pay of the workers and paid over to the union, only for those individual members who sign cards or statements asking that their membership dues be deducted from their wages. Even after the deduction has been provided for in that way, it is still revocable in that any member of a union who has requested that his dues be deducted may revoke that request and, if he does so, the company discontinues deducting that particular employee's union dues. So it is clear that it is the very minimum of what is known as union security. It is the least provision one can ask to further the cause of helping to retain union membership and making it possible for unions to get along with other important business rather than spending time on the details of collecting dues.
The idea of a check-off is not confined to unions. Most employers, whether government or private, make deductions of one kind or another from their employees. The best known form of check-off, and the one most widely practised, is that which comes under the Minister of Labour's colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, in the income tax deductions that take place at the source. Almost everyone in Canada whose income is in a bracket that makes him taxable at the end of the year finds that there is a deduction made from his cheque every week, every two weeks or every month. In addition to that, people request deductions for various charities to which they wish to make contributions, or for purchases of Canada savings bonds and so forth. Pension fund payments are also deducted at the source. In fact, I have seen statistics of firms where there are scores of items that are deducted, not from the same individual, but deducted by an employer in the course of his business.
Why there should be this resistance by management to this particular type of deduction is hard to understand, unless it is that somehow or other management likes to hold back on the full recognition of the rights of labour and the place of the trade union movement in our economy.
Many fine things are said in this house and on public platforms of all kinds throughout the country about the place of Canadian labour in our economy, about the right of our working people to their hard-won privileges, about their right to a decent standard of living and their right to security. That is all wrapped up, so far as workers are concerned, in their organized effort through their trade union movement, and they feel very

Industrial Relations
strongly that they should have the recognition implied in the voluntary revocable check-off.
I have no doubt that when a very important event takes place in the city of Toronto, beginning April 23, the Minister of Labour will be there and will extend his greetings, and the greetings of the government and people of Canada, to the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and the Canadian Labour Congress on the occasion of their merging into the Canadian Labour Congress. It will be a very important and significant event, and all of us who are related in any way to the labour movement are very proud of the step that is being taken. We feel that it will be for the good of workers generally and for the good of Canada that unity has been achieved between these two major labour bodies, and it augurs well for the future, not only because of the union that is taking place but because of the spirit in which it is being effected.
It seems to me that the Minister of Labour would feel much happier going to that convention-if he gets an invitation, as I am sure he will-if he could indicate to the new congress a few steps that have been taken this very year to show that the recognition of the labour movement consists not just of words, not just of the fine speech he will make from the rostrum if he goes there, but in legislation such as this that would mark a further step in national recognition of the place of the trade union movement in this country.
As I say, I have been pleased that in the past we have had the support, not only of all those on this side of the house but of a dozen to 15 or more Liberals, when this measure has come to a vote. I hope that this year the Minister of Labour will support it and that this piece of legislation, which recognizes the right of labour in a particular way, will be included in our national labour code.

Mr. Speaker, in the six years I have been sitting in this house this question of the compulsory check-off has come up quite often, practically every year. After a thorough study of the matter I have come to the conclusion that it is my duty to oppose this legislation.
I want to say first of all that I am in favour of trade unionism. Secondly, each worker should support his own union. Thirdly, that achievement should come about through an agreement between employee

and employer, and not through an act of parliament.
Here is what this legislation seeks to accomplish, and I quote section 1, paragraph 3:
Upon request of a trade union entitled to bargain collectively under this act on behalf of a unit of employees and upon receipt of a request in writing signed by any employee in such unit, the employer of such employee shall, until the employee in writing withdraws such request, periodically deduct, and pay out of the wages due to such employee to the person designated by the trade union to receive the same, the union dues of such employee.
I will come back later on to that last part, for I believe it is up to the worker to designate that person.
And the employer shall furnish to such trade union the names of the employees who have given and withdrawn such authority.
I do not agree at all with the sponsor of this bill when it comes to the means of effecting such social security. Since I have been sitting in this house I have often noticed that all groups represented here approve the principle of a bill but disagree on the way it should be carried out. If this legislation could bring about a greater measure of social security I would gladly vote for it, but I fear its adoption would have rather dire results.
The economic history of Canada shows that trade unionism plays a very important part, even an essential part in our industrial expansion. In my opinion, labour legislation derives its strength from the fact that it enables the members of a group or nation to obtain information on the matters under dispute. I agree with those who believe that unions have come to stay and if we want to protect them, we must give them the opportunity of extending their activity, and not hamper their work.
It is not by fostering disagreement between employers and workers that we will promote unity in trade unions. In that connection, I would like to quote an excerpt from "The Labour Problem in the Light of the Social Doctrine of the Church in Quebec":
Professional organizations.
In order to make their full contribution in the national economy, promote their professional interests and further their legitimate claims in the economic and social fields, workers must unite in strong professional organizations.
Every man is bound to ensure the protection and security of all his professional interests. He should strive to secure for himself and his family what he needs to lead a truly human life, sheltered from the uncertainties of the future. He must contribute to the welfare of his fellow citizens, particularly those who share with him common interests. It is his duty to co-operate toward the

restoration of a better balanced social order, while furthering the respect for justice in all labour, industrial and business activities. Alone, he cannot succeed. By uniting with his fellow workers, he will be able to discharge that imperious social duty. Under present circumstances, he has therefore a moral obligation to take an active part In professional organization.
And I now quote paragraph 106:
By striving to ensure unity and harmony between capital and labour, one is not hampering the work of trade unions; on the contrary, such an effort is essential to ensure a careful and courageous evolution towards the adequate development of the labouring class; such an evolution will bring permanent and stable results.
In brief, the proposed legislation does not favour in the least the labouring class but does favour the union leader who wishes to ensure the perenniality of his salary.
Mr. Speaker, I have learned and I have taught that a good engineer, when undertaking to change the topography of a piece of land, must accept the ensuing consequences.
The same goes for any attempt to change the basis of the legislation and regulations pertaining to employers and employees.
I am also convinced that the standard of living of our working class can easily be compared to that of the labouring class of other countries.
This is due to the fact that our legislation has done more than any other to further the development of the labour movement in this country. Why should we complicate by legislation the friendly relations between employers and workers?
If improvements have been so consistent, we owe it to the understanding and the intelligence of our labouring class, supplemented by a wise legislation contributing to the application of principles capable of promoting the development of the labouring class.
If I have not taken part in this debate up to now, it is because, being the representative of a predominantly agricultural district, I had decided to abstain from speaking; however, having received from a mining organization of my province a request to oppose this bill, I felt it my duty to express my opinion after a careful study of the matter.
I do not believe it is fair to ask employers to do the work which the unions themselves should do. This procedure could very well bring about indifference on the part of the worker as regards his union since he would no longer be in contact with his association. Moreover this would seem to infer that the worker would not pay his dues willingly.
I am too well acquainted with the workers of the province of Quebec to allow such doubts
Industrial Relations
to be cast upon the way in which they discharge their obligations. I would like to quote further, in this connection, from "The Labour Problem in Quebec", page 12.
A number of facts observed by us among the working people of Quebec are such as to give rise to real admiration because they reveal the riches of the worker. Our city families, our workers have fine qualities. Could we remain silent in the face of the sacrifices which the working class father constantly undergoes on behalf of his wife and children? How could we do justice to the devotion of those many wonderful mothers through whose strength and resourcefulness families find comfort in adversity and a livelihood from a limited budget? Through an appropriate education and in co-operation with their husbands they find the means of bringing up their children in a Christian way and of preparing them for urban living.
We have noted that our province has become largely urban in character. The adaptation of the countryman to city living is difficult. The worker and his family are beset with dangers, but resistance is taking shape. Class consciousness is developing among our workers; they demand that their rights be respected. Faced with this rising force some are worried, others remain confident and these are the more numerous.
Let us assume that there are in this country one million workers paying two dollars monthly. That means two million dollars per month that the employers alone would be called upon to pay over to the union treasury.
It seems to me that that is contrary to the right of the individual to do what he pleases with what is rightfully his.
In carrying out my professional duties I have always tried to let responsibilities remain where they belong. In this instance these responsibilities are those of the employer, the worker and the province concerned.
And when I say that this is the business of the employer and the worker, I quote again from the publication entitled "The Labour Problem in Quebec", page 50:
Relations with employees
The true employer, whatever the number of his employees, realizes his obligations as head of a working community. He appreciates his employees, not only for their physical strength or their productive ability, but also for their co-operation in a common endeavour and, particularly, for their dignity as men and Christians. A Christian employer is known by his determination to create a happy atmosphere in the enterprise, by his genuine solicitude for his associates in the labouring effort, by the genuine charity he shows towards them.
As regards the worker, I quote from page 34 of the same book:
Action required of the ones primarily interested.
The rehabilitation of the worker's status can be achieved properly only if workers have a noble and truly Christian appreciation of themselves and only if they are fundamentally prepared to co-operate and to help. Before counting on the

Industrial Relations
help of others, they must rely on their own efforts, on their own defence, on their mutual assistance, in the application of which the basic element is the feeling of close solidarity between those who give and those who take. They shall therefore be the primary makers of their improved situation, failing which the best reform projects cannot achieve the desired results.
Moreover, the province should make sure that it can exercise its rights. To this effect, I wish to quote, from page 61 of the same publication, an excerpt dealing with the role of the state as between employers and workers.
The workers, who are primarily interested, the employers, the members of the liberal professions and the educators who, in varying degrees, have a considerable influence over the life of the workers, should aim to contribute, each in his own way, to the rehabilitation of the labour conditions, and to "improve gradually and by peaceful means the physical and spiritual status of the working man". In their service, the state wields authority in order to place all, and therefore the workers, within easy reach of living conditions corresponding to their dignity. While it is not part of the state's duty to substitute its own action to that of the individuals and the lower level groups, it is within its province to take particular care of the weaker members.
I believe that very few Quebec companies fall under the federal labour code and that it would be more advisable to let the provincial governments legislate in this matter. I also believe that the only ones who could solve the problem to the advantage of those involved are the workers and employers themselves.
In my opinion, union security, whatever it may be, should continue to be discussed
by the company and the union, with a view to eliminating all coercion.
Moreover, it would become increasingly difficult for the provincial governments who, until now, have resisted all union pressure to write the check-off into their labour code,- it would become increasingly difficult, I repeat, to maintain their opposition to this request, which scarcely tends to improve industrial relations.
For all those reasons, I shall oppose the adoption of this act as long as the workers of my province have not convinced me that it is needed.
